A silent eligibility trace \u2013 initiated by synaptic activity and transformed into synaptic strengthening by later action of dopamine \u2013 has been hypothesized to explain the retroactive effect of dopamine in reinforcing past behaviour. We tested this hypothesis by measuring time\u2010dependent modulation of synaptic plasticity by dopamine in adult mouse striatum, using whole\u2010cell recordings. Presynaptic activity followed by postsynaptic action potentials (pre\u2013post) caused spike\u2010timing\u2010dependent long\u2010term depression in D1\u2010expressing neurons, but not in D2 neurons, and not if postsynaptic activity followed presynaptic activity. Subsequent experiments focused on D1 neurons. Applying a dopamine D1 receptor agonist during induction of pre\u2013post plasticity caused long\u2010term potentiation. This long\u2010term potentiation was hidden by long\u2010term depression occurring concurrently and was unmasked when long\u2010term depression blocked an L\u2010type calcium channel antagonist. Long\u2010term potentiation was blocked by a Ca\n                    <jats:sup>2+<\/jats:sup>\n                    \u2010permeable\n                    <jats:styled-content style=\"fixed-case\">AMPA<\/jats:styled-content>\n                    receptor antagonist but not by an\n                    <jats:styled-content style=\"fixed-case\">NMDA<\/jats:styled-content>\n                    antagonist or an L\u2010type calcium channel antagonist. Pre\u2013post stimulation caused transient elevation of rectification \u2013 a marker for expression of Ca\n                    <jats:sup>2+<\/jats:sup>\n                    \u2010permeable\n                    <jats:styled-content style=\"fixed-case\">AMPA<\/jats:styled-content>\n                    receptors \u2013 for 2\u20134\u2010s after stimulation. To test for an eligibility trace, dopamine was uncaged at specific time points before and after pre\u2010 and postsynaptic conjunction of activity. Dopamine caused potentiation selectively at synapses that were active 2\u2010s before dopamine release, but not at earlier or later times. Our results provide direct evidence for a silent eligibility trace in the synapses of striatal neurons. This dopamine\u2010timing\u2010dependent plasticity may play a central role in reinforcement learning.\n
